situation:
You are the Customer Relations Coordinator and the Installation Team Lead at IRONLATCH, a home security installation cooperative owned entirely by the technicians, schedulers, and support staff who work there. IRONLATCH designs, installs, and monitors alarm, camera, and smart-lock systems for homeowners across the region, with installation requests peaking sharply during the spring and summer home-closing season. The cooperative's general manager (judge), elected annually by the membership, has asked the two of you to meet about a marketing problem that surfaced this week and now needs a recommendation before the next board update.

Eighteen months ago IRONLATCH entered a referral partnership with PARKROW REALTY, a real estate brokerage whose agents refer newly closing homebuyers to IRONLATCH for security installations at move-in. To promote the partnership, a member of IRONLATCH's marketing staff arranged a flat fee for one of Parkrow's senior agents to record a testimonial praising IRONLATCH's crews, which then ran on the company's website, in social ads, and in every closing packet Parkrow handed to buyers. The payment was never disclosed, and the arrangement is a personnel matter still confidential from the rest of the staff.

A homeowner who signed a monitoring contract after watching the testimonial later learned, through an unrelated news story about paid endorsements, that the agent had been compensated, and complained to the state consumer protection office. IRONLATCH's own review confirmed the testimonial ran for eleven months, appeared in roughly six hundred closing packets, and was never labeled as sponsored. The office closed its inquiry after IRONLATCH pulled the testimonial and began labeling every paid endorsement going forward.

What remains is what to do about customers who signed contracts while the undisclosed testimonial was running, and what to do about Parkrow itself. The referral channel now accounts for close to a third of new installations and the member hours tied to them, a volume the membership has set a goal of growing further next year. Parkrow has offered to keep referring buyers, with its agent re-recording a properly labeled endorsement, but only if IRONLATCH gives Parkrow's marketing director a standing seat reviewing any future materials that mention the brokerage before they run.

The general manager (judge) wants a recommendation on how far back the cooperative should reach to make things right with customers who acted on the undisclosed testimonial, and on whether to accept Parkrow's condition for keeping the partnership alive. The recommendation should weigh what the cooperative owes those customers, what continuing or ending the Parkrow relationship would mean for installation volume and member pay, and how the correction should be communicated to staff and to customers alike.

The general manager (judge) will greet you both at the start of the meeting and ask to hear your ideas. After you present your recommendation for handling the affected customers and the future of the Parkrow partnership and answer any follow-up questions, the general manager (judge) will thank you both for your work and bring the meeting to a close.
